name: Australia
traditionNote: A Westminster common-law federation: the binding law is Acts of Parliament plus judge-made precedent, so you normally need both the consolidated statute and the cases interpreting it, and you need to know whether the subject belongs to the Commonwealth or to a State.
summary: Law is made by the Commonwealth Parliament and by the parliaments of six States and two self-governing Territories, with ministers and agencies making delegated legislation under powers those parliaments confer. Commonwealth Acts, legislative instruments, notifiable instruments, the Constitution and the Commonwealth Gazette are all published on one site, the Federal Register of Legislation, run by the Office of Parliamentary Counsel under the Legislation Act 2003; States and Territories each run their own equivalent register. A Commonwealth Act becomes law on Royal Assent and, unless it says otherwise, commences 28 days later; a legislative instrument is not enforceable until it is registered on the Register, and most instruments sunset automatically about ten years after commencement. The authentic text is the authorised electronic version on the Register (or the State equivalent) - the register version, not a printed reprint or a commercial copy. Case law is the other half of the law: judgments of the High Court, Federal Court and State supreme courts are published free by the courts themselves and mirrored on AustLII.
hierarchy: The Commonwealth Constitution (s 9 of the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900, alterable only by referendum under s 128)
Acts of the Commonwealth Parliament, which prevail over inconsistent State law under s 109
Commonwealth legislative and notifiable instruments (regulations, rules, determinations, orders) made under an Act
State and Territory constitutions and constitution acts
Acts of the State and Territory parliaments
State and Territory subordinate legislation (regulations, statutory rules, subordinate laws)
Local government by-laws and local laws made under State authority
The common law of Australia - binding precedent descending from the High Court - which fills gaps but yields to valid statute

gazette.name: Commonwealth of Australia Gazette
gazette.authority: Office of Parliamentary Counsel, published on the Federal Register of Legislation
gazette.coverage: 1901-present. Notices published from 1 October 2012 onward are individually searchable electronic documents; 1901 to December 2012 exists as scanned PDF issues.
gazette.desc: The Commonwealth's notice of record: proclamations, commencement and appointment notices, departmental and court notices, and anything else a Commonwealth Act requires to be gazetted. Since 2012 it is electronic-only and lives inside the legislation register rather than as a separate publication, so a gazette notice is searched exactly like an Act.
gazette.howto: Use the register's browse or search with the collection filter set to Gazette (https://www.legislation.gov.au/search/collection(Gazette)/status(InForce)); for anything before October 2012 go to the historic list at https://www.legislation.gov.au/gazettes/historic and open the scanned issue for the relevant date.
gazette.note: Several agencies run their own specialist gazettes (for example in employment, business and Indigenous affairs) that are published separately and are not all mirrored here.

constitution.name: Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act
constitution.authority: Office of Parliamentary Counsel / Attorney-General's Department, on the Federal Register of Legislation
constitution.coverage: Royal Assent 9 July 1900, commenced 1 January 1901; the register text incorporates all eight successful referendum alterations, the last dating from 1977
constitution.desc: The Constitution proper is section 9 of a United Kingdom Act of 1900; the covering clauses that precede it are part of that Act and remain in the text. This register entry is the authorised electronic version, chaptered as Parliament, Executive Government, Judicature, Finance and Trade, the States, New States, Miscellaneous and Alteration.
constitution.howto: Open the entry and pick a chapter from the contents panel, or use the download control for the whole text as PDF or Word; the version date shown (29 July 1977) is the date of the last alteration, not a currency problem.
constitution.note: The register also lists the Constitution under the older identifier C2013Q00005, and https://www.legislation.gov.au/constitution is a plain-language landing page that links through to this text.

sources.name: Federal Register of Legislation
sources.authority: Office of Parliamentary Counsel (OPC), under the Legislation Act 2003
sources.coverage: All Commonwealth Acts in force and their compilations, plus legislative and notifiable instruments; authorised versions of every legislative instrument made since 1 January 2005 and of pre-2005 instruments still in force on 1 January 2008
sources.desc: The single authorised whole-of-government site for Commonwealth law: Constitution, Acts, legislative instruments, notifiable instruments, gazettes, administrative arrangements orders, prerogative instruments and Norfolk Island legislation. This is the site to use rather than any department's own copy of its Act.
sources.howto: Search by title, ID or full text, then narrow with the facets on the results page: collection (Act, Legislative instrument, Gazette), status (in force / no longer in force), principal vs amending, and portfolio. On a title's page the Versions control gives point-in-time compilations and the 'as made' original.
sources.note: There is no published bulk-download or open API; researchers who need datasets have historically had to scrape the site.

sources.name: Federal Register of Legislation - advanced search
sources.coverage: Same holdings as the register, with date-based and status-based filtering
sources.desc: The faceted search behind the register, and the fastest route to a specific version of a specific instrument. It is the only place that reliably answers 'what did this section say on that date'.
sources.howto: Set the temporal option to 'As at' a date, or 'Between' two dates, and tick 'Include superseded versions'; combine with collection, classification (regulations, rules, court rules, by-laws) and portfolio filters, then sort by relevance or registration date.

sources.name: Legislative instruments (Federal Register of Legislation)
sources.authority: Office of Parliamentary Counsel (OPC), under the Legislation Act 2003
sources.coverage: All registered Commonwealth legislative instruments; in-force, amending and no-longer-in-force browse lists
sources.desc: Regulations, rules, determinations and orders made under Commonwealth Acts. Registration here is not a courtesy: under the Legislation Act 2003 an unregistered legislative instrument is not enforceable, which makes this list definitive rather than indicative.
sources.howto: Browse 'principal in force' for the instrument you want (amending instruments are listed separately), or search the register with the collection filter set to Legislative instrument and the classification filter set to Regulations or Rules.
sources.note: Most legislative instruments sunset automatically about ten years after commencement unless remade or exempted, so an instrument you found in an old textbook may simply have expired.

sources.name: Bills and Legislation - Parliament of Australia
sources.authority: Department of the House of Representatives / Department of the Senate
sources.coverage: Bills before the current Parliament and archived bills from earlier parliaments, with progress through both chambers
sources.desc: Where law is tracked before it becomes law: bill text at each stage, explanatory memoranda, amendments moved, second reading speeches and the date each chamber agreed. A bill becomes an Act only when both houses pass it in identical form and the Governor-General assents.
sources.howto: Use the bills search and filter by title, chamber, portfolio or introduction date; open a bill's homepage for the 'Progress' tab, the explanatory memorandum and the text as introduced and as passed. Once assented, follow the link across to the Federal Register of Legislation for the operative text.
sources.note: A bill listed here has no legal effect; only the assented Act on the Register does.

sources.name: Bills Digests - Parliamentary Library
sources.authority: Parliamentary Library, Department of Parliamentary Services
sources.desc: Independent plain-English analyses of bills written for members of Parliament: purpose, background, key provisions, financial implications and the arguments raised against them. The fastest way to understand why a statute is written the way it is.
sources.howto: Browse the alphabetical list or search by bill title; digests are also linked from each bill's homepage in the bills database.
sources.note: Analysis only, written at the time of the bill - it is not updated as the Act is later amended.

sources.name: High Court of Australia - Judgments
sources.coverage: Full-text judgments of the High Court, listed by year, with the court's own short judgment summaries issued alongside them
sources.desc: The apex court for the whole federation: it is the final court of appeal from every State and Territory court and the only court that can definitively settle constitutional questions and s 109 inconsistency. Its decisions bind every other Australian court.
sources.howto: Under Cases and Judgments, the Judgments page lists decisions by year and links the full reasons; most judgments are accompanied by a short official judgment summary explaining what was decided. The sibling Special Leave page (https://www.hcourt.gov.au/cases-and-judgments/special-leave) tracks applications for special leave to appeal, which is how nearly every case reaches the Court. AustLII carries the same judgments if the court site is unreachable.
sources.note: For citation in court the authorised report is the Commonwealth Law Reports (CLR); the free court version carries the medium-neutral citation [YYYY] HCA n. The site is served from a CDN that drops many automated and non-Australian requests, so it can time out for a scripted client while being live in a browser.

sources.name: Federal Law Search - Federal Court of Australia
sources.coverage: All cases commenced from 1 January 1984; full-text orders from 2005 (some from 2004); judgments from 1995 in HTML/Word and 1977-1994 as searchable PDF
sources.desc: The Federal Court decides most Commonwealth statutory litigation - corporations, competition, tax, migration, intellectual property, native title. Federal Law Search gives the case file, parties, hearing dates and orders; the court's Digital Law Library holds the judgments themselves.
sources.howto: Search Federal Law Search by party name or file number for the docket, hearing dates and orders; for the reasons for judgment go to the court's Digital Law Library judgments section at https://www.fedcourt.gov.au/digital-law-library/judgments, or look the medium-neutral citation ([YYYY] FCA n or [YYYY] FCAFC n) up on AustLII.
sources.note: Suppression and non-publication orders mean some files and judgments are restricted or redacted. The site sits behind a Cloudflare challenge, so scripted requests get a 403 interstitial even though the pages are live in a browser.

sources.name: Australasian Legal Information Institute (AustLII)
sources.authority: AustLII Foundation Limited, a joint facility of the UTS and UNSW law faculties (established 1995)
sources.coverage: Commonwealth, State and Territory legislation and case law across hundreds of courts and tribunals, plus treaties, law reform reports and law journals; New Zealand and Pacific material via sister institutes
sources.desc: Not a government publisher, but in practice the single most-used free legal database in Australia and often the only place a tribunal decision or an older judgment is findable at all. Its consolidated Acts are secondary copies of the official registers, updated on its own schedule.
sources.howto: Use the front-page search across all databases, or pick a jurisdiction database (for example the Commonwealth Consolidated Acts, or a court's judgment series) and browse alphabetically; the NoteUp function finds later cases that cited a judgment. The Australian Treaties Library sits at https://www.austlii.edu.au/database-treaties.html.
sources.note: Explicitly unofficial: for the operative text of a statute or instrument, check the government register before relying on AustLII's copy.

sources.name: Treaties - Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
sources.authority: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT)
sources.coverage: Treaty actions Australia has taken - signature, ratification, accession, entry into force and termination - including the Australian Treaty Series (ATS) and treaties signed but not yet in force
sources.desc: DFAT is the department responsible for Australia's treaty making and the official source for treaty status and treaty text. Australia is dualist: a treaty binds Australia internationally but changes domestic law only when Parliament enacts implementing legislation, so a treaty is not itself a source of enforceable domestic rights. Proposed treaty actions are tabled in Parliament with a national interest analysis and scrutinised by the Joint Standing Committee on Treaties before Australia is bound.
sources.howto: Start from DFAT's treaties pages for treaty-making process, status and treaty-action lists. For the full text of a concluded treaty the reliable free route is AustLII's Australian Treaties Library (https://www.austlii.edu.au/database-treaties.html), which carries the Australian Treaty Series and the national interest analyses; for a treaty currently before Parliament use the Joint Standing Committee on Treaties at https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Committees/Joint/Treaties.
sources.note: DFAT's separate Australian Treaties Database at info.dfat.gov.au/treaties is offline - the host returns a Cloudflare 522 on every path and has not been successfully archived since November 2025 - so do not rely on links to it. AustLII's Australian Treaties Library is the working substitute for full texts. dfat.gov.au itself is served from a CDN that refuses many automated and non-Australian requests, so a client-side fetch of this URL may time out even though the page is live.

sources.name: NSW Legislation
sources.authority: Parliamentary Counsel's Office of New South Wales
sources.coverage: NSW Acts back to 1824, statutory instruments, bills and their explanatory notes, with point-in-time historical versions
sources.desc: The official NSW register and the source of authorised NSW legislation. NSW is the largest State by population, so a great deal of everyday Australian law - crime, land, health, roads - is found here rather than on the Commonwealth register.
sources.howto: Search or browse by title for the in-force version, then use the historical versions list for the text at a past date; 'As made' PDFs give the Act or instrument exactly as enacted, with the bill and explanatory note kept separately.

sources.name: NSW Government Gazette
sources.authority: Parliamentary Counsel's Office of New South Wales, under s 45C of the Interpretation Act 1987 (NSW)
sources.coverage: Browsable and searchable back to 2001 - the year selector on the catalogue runs 2001 to the current year and 2001 issues are present as scanned PDFs; issues before 2001 are held by the State Library of NSW and digitised on the National Library's Trove
sources.desc: The permanent public record of NSW government, local council and other notices where legislation requires gazettal - compulsory acquisitions, appointments, planning and rural fire notices among them. Included here as the model for how the States publish notices, since each State runs its own gazette.
sources.howto: Use the site search, or open the catalogue and pick a year from the 2001-to-present selector, then a month; issues are also grouped by notice category (Crown Land, Planning and Heritage, Roads and Transport and about nine others). The ordinary issue is published each Friday, with special issues on other days for urgent matters.
sources.note: Lodging a notice requires an account with multi-factor authentication; reading and searching does not.

sources.name: Victorian Legislation
sources.authority: Office of the Chief Parliamentary Counsel and the Parliament of Victoria
sources.coverage: Acts and statutory rules in force with amendments incorporated, as-made versions, repealed and revoked instruments, bills, and historical Acts 1851-1995
sources.desc: Victoria's official legislation site, covering both Acts and statutory rules (the Victorian term for regulations). The historical 1851-1995 collection makes it one of the better State sites for older material.
sources.howto: Search by title or keyword and pick 'In force' for the current consolidation or 'As made' for the original; the Legislative Information section links out to the Victoria Government Gazette for notices and commencement dates.

sources.name: Queensland Legislation
sources.authority: Office of the Queensland Parliamentary Counsel (OQPC)
sources.coverage: Bills, Acts as passed, subordinate legislation as made, and point-in-time reprints; HTML versions from 2016 onward, PDF throughout
sources.desc: Queensland's authorised legislation site. Its point-in-time reprint system is the clearest of the State registers for reconstructing what a provision said on a particular day.
sources.howto: Search for the Act, then choose a reprint by date from its version list; 'As passed' and 'As made' give the original text. XML of legislation is available on request from OQPC.

sources.name: Western Australian Legislation
sources.authority: Parliamentary Counsel's Office, Government of Western Australia
sources.coverage: Acts in force, ceased Acts, Acts as passed and reprints; subsidiary legislation; bills from 1997; current and historical Government Gazettes
sources.desc: Western Australia's official register, and unusual among the State sites in hosting the State Government Gazette in the same place as the legislation, so notices and the instruments they commence sit side by side.
sources.howto: Browse Acts alphabetically or by year for the current reprint, use the Subsidiary Legislation section for regulations and rules, and the Gazette section to find the notice that commenced an Act.

sources.name: Documenting a Democracy
sources.authority: Museum of Australian Democracy with the National Archives of Australia and the State and Territory archives
sources.coverage: 110 foundational documents from the colonial period to the late twentieth century, arranged by jurisdiction
sources.desc: Digitised images and transcripts of the documents that created Australian government: the colonial constitution acts, the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900, letters patent, statutes of Westminster adoption and the Australia Acts. Where the register gives you the operative text, this gives you the original instrument.
sources.howto: Pick a jurisdiction (Commonwealth or a State) from the front page, then open a document for its scanned image, transcript and a short explanation of what it did.
sources.note: An archived site - no longer updated, and some interactive features no longer work.

findLaw.task: Find the current consolidated text of a Commonwealth Act
findLaw.steps: Search the Federal Register of Legislation by the Act's title, open the result and take the latest compilation - the register shows the compilation date and the amendments included. Compilations, not the original 'as made' version, are what is currently in force.

findLaw.task: See what changed, or read a provision as it stood on a past date
findLaw.steps: On the Act's register page use the Versions control to list every compilation with its start and end dates, or use the advanced search with 'As at' a date and 'Include superseded versions' ticked. Each compilation carries an endnotes table listing the amending Acts.
findLaw.source: Federal Register of Legislation - advanced search

findLaw.task: Find a regulation, rule or other legislative instrument
findLaw.steps: Browse the legislative instruments list, or search the register with the collection filter set to Legislative instrument and classification set to Regulations, Rules, Court rules or By-laws. If an instrument is not on the register it is not enforceable, and check whether it has sunset.
findLaw.source: Federal Register of Legislation - legislative instruments

findLaw.steps: For constitutional and final-appeal questions open the High Court's Judgments page, which lists decisions by year with the full reasons and the court's short judgment summaries; for federal statutory litigation use the Federal Court's Digital Law Library. To search every Australian court and tribunal at once, including State courts, use AustLII and its NoteUp function to see which later cases cited the one you have.
findLaw.source: High Court of Australia, with AustLII for cross-court searching

findLaw.steps: Search the Parliament of Australia bills database by title or introduction date, open the bill's homepage for its progress through both chambers, the explanatory memorandum and the text as introduced and as passed, then read the Parliamentary Library's Bills Digest for the background.
findLaw.source: Bills and Legislation - Parliament of Australia

findLaw.steps: Go to the register of the jurisdiction that has the subject - NSW, Victoria, Queensland and Western Australia each publish their own authorised Acts and subordinate legislation - and search there rather than on the Commonwealth register. Where a Commonwealth Act and a State Act conflict on the same subject, s 109 of the Constitution makes the Commonwealth Act prevail to the extent of the inconsistency.
findLaw.source: NSW Legislation (and the equivalent State and Territory registers)

findLaw.task: Find an official notice, proclamation or commencement
findLaw.steps: Search the Commonwealth gazette collection on the register with the collection filter set to Gazette; for notices before October 2012 open the scanned issue for the relevant date from the historic gazette list. State notices are in that State's own gazette.

subnational: Australia is a federation, and subnational law is a large share of all Australian law: the six States (New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia, Tasmania) and the two self-governing mainland Territories (Australian Capital Territory, Northern Territory) each have their own parliament, their own Acts and subordinate legislation, their own gazette and their own courts. Each jurisdiction runs its own official register, drafted and published by that jurisdiction's Parliamentary Counsel: legislation.nsw.gov.au, legislation.vic.gov.au, legislation.qld.gov.au and legislation.wa.gov.au for the four largest, plus https://www.legislation.tas.gov.au/ for Tasmania, https://www.legislation.act.gov.au/ for the ACT and https://legislation.nt.gov.au/ for the Northern Territory. Coverage and start dates differ sharply - Tasmania's consolidations begin at 1 February 1997 and its statutory rules at May 1998, the ACT register reaches back to 1911, NSW to 1824 - so for older State material you may need the State library or archives rather than the register. Local councils make by-laws under State authority; these are generally published by the council or in the State gazette, not on the State legislation register.
caveats: Only the authorised electronic version on the government register is the authentic text: the Federal Register of Legislation carries authorised versions of every legislative instrument made since 1 January 2005 and of pre-2005 instruments still in force on 1 January 2008, and older material can be an unauthorised scan. AustLII and commercial services such as the subscription databases used in practice are not official publishers, however good their coverage; their consolidations are secondary copies on their own update cycles. 'As made' and 'as passed' text is the original and is almost never the law today - you want the current compilation or reprint. For court citation the authorised law reports (the Commonwealth Law Reports for the High Court) outrank the free medium-neutral versions on court websites, and suppression orders mean some judgments and case files are restricted. Law is published in English only; there is no other authentic language version, and Documenting a Democracy is an archived site that is no longer maintained.
